Students at schools with five or more retailers within 800 metres had higher odds of current smoking than students at schools with none (odds ratio 1.31, 95 percent CI 1.08 to 1.59) after adjustment for school socioeconomic status, remoteness and student age and sex. There was no clear dose-response between one and four retailers. The association was similar in metropolitan and regional schools. Cross-sectional data cannot establish whether retailers locate near schools with more demand."},{"title":"Retailer density near schools and student vaping: evidence from two survey waves","authors":"Oduya-Kristensen R, Blanchard-Owusu E","year":2024,"venue":"Adolescent Risk Studies Quarterly","doi":"10.5555/arsq.2024.0071","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using two waves of a school health survey (2021 and 2023) linked to licensed retailer locations, we examined current vaping among 18,700 students. In 2023, students at schools with three or more retailers within 800 metres had higher odds of current vaping (odds ratio 1.22, 95 percent CI 1.03 to 1.45); in 2021 the association was weaker and its interval included 1. Adjustment for school socioeconomic status reduced both associations by about a third. Vape-only retailers were not licensed in the study period and could not be counted."},{"title":"Outlet density and youth smoking after adjustment for area deprivation: a cross-sectional study in three cities","authors":"Guerrero-Stanek L, Mwale-Fitzgerald T","year":2017,"venue":"Urban Health Analyses","doi":"10.5555/uha.2017.0233","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In three cities, we related the density of tobacco outlets around 96 secondary schools to current smoking among 14,900 students. The unadjusted association was strong (odds ratio 1.62 for the highest against the lowest density quartile), but after adjustment for neighbourhood deprivation it fell to 1.09 (95 percent CI 0.88 to 1.35). Deprivation was associated with both outlet density and smoking. The authors caution that density limits may do less than expected if deprivation drives both, and recommend analyses that model deprivation carefully."},{"title":"Buffer size and exposure measurement for retail environment studies around schools","authors":"Sato-Warrington H, Delgado-Ansah M","year":2019,"venue":"Spatial Epidemiology Letters","doi":"10.5555/sel.2019.0142","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared retailer counts within 400, 800 and 1,600 metres of 150 schools, using road network distance and straight-line distance. Counts within 800 metres by road network distance best reflected the routes students reported walking between school and home or shops. Straight-line buffers overstated exposure for schools near rivers, rail lines and highways. Associations with student smoking were strongest for the 800 metre road network buffer. About one school in five had no retailer within 800 metres, which should be modelled as a separate category rather than as a low count."},{"title":"Where students buy cigarettes and vapes: purchase locations reported in a state school survey","authors":"Novak-Idowu F, Harlan-Tse B","year":2022,"venue":"Adolescent Risk Studies Quarterly","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Among 2,640 students who reported current smoking or vaping in a state school survey, 36 percent of smokers and 44 percent of vapers said they had bought their own product in the past month, mostly from convenience stores and service stations. Students aged under 16 were less likely to report buying their own product and more likely to obtain it from friends or siblings. Purchasing near school was reported by 18 percent of those who bought their own. The survey did not verify purchase locations."},{"title":"Licensing caps on tobacco outlets near schools: an evaluation five years after introduction","authors":"Morrow-Adebayo J, Linde-Chukwu O, Pereira-Vance S","year":2025,"venue":"Tobacco Control Policy Evaluations","doi":"10.5555/tcpe.2025.0014","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A state capped new tobacco licences within 500 metres of schools in 2019. Five years later the number of licensed outlets within 500 metres of schools had fallen by 23 percent, mostly through closures rather than refusals. Current smoking among students fell in both capped and comparison areas, and the difference in the decline between areas was small and imprecise (1.4 percentage points, 95 percent CI -0.9 to 3.7). The evaluation could not separate the cap from other tobacco control measures introduced in the same period."},{"title":"Measuring current smoking and vaping in school surveys: agreement with saliva cotinine","authors":"Kimura-Blake D, Fashola-Ruiz A","year":2016,"venue":"Survey Methods in Public Health","doi":"10.5555/smph.2016.0088","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"School surveys rely on students' own reports of smoking and vaping. In a validation sub-study of 1,120 students from 40 schools, self-reported current smoking agreed well with saliva cotinine (sensitivity 0.87, specificity 0.96), but self-reported vaping could not be validated because cotinine does not separate nicotine sources. Reporting was more accurate when surveys were completed without teachers present and when students were told that answers could not be traced to them. The authors recommend defining current use as any use in the past 30 days and reporting smoking and vaping separately."}]}
